title: Usage Limit Handoff
eyebrow: Revised design for approval · keep work handed off on every surface · nothing built yet

short.lead: You asked for work to be saved and handed off at 90% usage, so another Claude account can continue it, and for it to work in the terminal, the desktop app, cloud sessions and on your phone. I tested what each surface exposes. Not every surface can report a 90% reading. Only the terminal's status line (the bar of live information at the bottom of the screen) reports your usage percentage, and cloud sessions don't run a status line at all. What does run everywhere is a hook (a small script Claude Code runs automatically) that fires at the end of every reply. So this design no longer waits for 90%. Every reply that changed files ends with the work committed, pushed and described in a short handoff note, so no work is left unsaved when the limit hits. This replaces open issue #140 ("auto create a handoff document at 95% usage and commit all current changes"). The first version of this page is kept as docs/plans/2026-10-27-usage-limit-handoff.html.
short.hint: Tap a step to see exactly what was tested and the evidence.
items: The status line documentation (code.claude.com/docs/en/statusline.md, "Available data") lists rate_limits.five_hour.used_percentage and rate_limits.seven_day.used_percentage for Pro and Max subscribers. A plugin can't set a status line itself (docs/3-state/ProjectState.md line 106); the installer would have to.

In this cloud session I set up a status line that saved the data it received to a file, refreshing every 5 seconds. It never ran across about 15 replies, so cloud sessions don't run a status line. The session record does carry a rate-limit status ("allowed" normally, "allowed_warning" near the limit, per the Agent SDK reference). But Anthropic decides when that warning appears, and no hook can read it. Your phone drives either a cloud session like this one or a Remote Control session running Claude Code on your computer, so it inherits those two cases.
Shows a usage ring, not a percentage to hooks

The desktop documentation shows a usage ring next to the model picker and never mentions running a status line. I couldn't test it: this session is bound to your Windows desktop app, but the app wasn't connected when I tried. The suggested design doesn't depend on it.
Only needed if you pick option B under Choices, the optional 90% warning in the terminal.
The end-of-reply hook runs on every surface

The hooks documentation says the same hook events fire in the terminal, IDE extensions, the desktop app and cloud sessions. I've seen it run: house-rules' end-of-reply (Stop) hook blocked one of my replies in this cloud thread today, and docs/desktop-verification.md records it verified on your Windows desktop app on 2026-09-07. A separate hook, StopFailure, fires when a reply fails because of a rate limit. It can't be tested without actually hitting a limit, so the design doesn't rely on it.
Pick one answer for each question under Choices (approach, note and pickup), then send the approval line.
Send "Design approved: usage limit handoff" with your picks, for example "1A 2A 3A", or tell me what to change.

changes: keep
Commit and push rules (rules/detail/commit-branches.md)
Saving uses the existing rules, with no new permission.

On any branch other than main, I already commit and push without asking. If you are on main, or on a branch of yours rather than one of mine, the save first creates a new branch whose name starts with AjsAgent/, as the rules already require.
keep
End-of-reply hook (scripts/hook.py, Stop)
The new check joins the existing Stop hook instead of adding a new hook.
That hook already blocks a reply once and sends it back with a reason, which is the same mechanism the new check needs.
chg
Save check (scripts/hook.py, Stop)
A reply that leaves changed files uncommitted, unpushed or undescribed is sent back once to finish saving.
Changed files can sit uncommitted between replies, so a limit that hits leaves them only on that machine or in that cloud container.

Before a reply ends, the hook checks three things: that no changes are left uncommitted, that the branch is pushed, and that the handoff note is newer than the last commit. If any check fails, the reply is sent back once, with the reason, to finish saving. A reply that changed nothing is never blocked.
HOUSE_RULES_HANDOFF=off turns it off. The hook only checks; the commit, push and note are mine, so commit messages stay meaningful.
chg
Handoff note (docs/5-today/handoff-<branch>.md)
One short note per branch, rewritten in place each time, not a new file per reply.

Five lines: what the work is for, where it stands, the next step, anything unverified, and the issue numbers. It reuses the shape of docs/handoff-2026-10-15.md, cut down so updating it costs little usage. Following your standing rule, the note never carries a published page link, a session link or any Claude credit, and the save check refuses a note that does.
chg
Pickup (scripts/hook.py, SessionStart)
A session that opens on a branch with a handoff note loads the note and says so first.
This works on any account that has the plugin and access to the repo, because the note is in the pushed branch, not on the machine.
chg
Rule text, docs, tests and version
One sentence in rules/house-rules.md, a docs/4-systems/ page, verify.py cases and a version bump.

verify.py replays a Stop event with uncommitted changes, with an unpushed branch, with a stale note, and with nothing changed. The version is set at merge time: main is at 2.73.1, the background-tracking build takes a 2.73.x patch and the restructure pull request takes 2.74.0, so this is expected to be 2.75.0.
choices: approach
When should work be saved and handed off?
A
Always: every reply that changed files ends saved
Works on every surface, because it needs only the end-of-reply hook. Costs a commit and a short note update on replies that changed files.
B
Always, plus a 90% warning in the terminal
Adds the installer status line, which tells me to wrap up at 90%. It works only in the terminal; desktop is untested and cloud has none.
C
Only at 90%, as first proposed
Fails your requirement: it can't fire in cloud sessions or from your phone, and is untested in the desktop app.
Option A never depends on reading usage, so there is no surface where it silently doesn't fire. Option B's extra warning is harmless, but it only helps in the terminal.
note
Who keeps the handoff note current?
A
I update it as part of saving
The note says what the next step is and why, which is what lets your other account start at once. It costs a few lines of output per saving reply.
B
The hook writes it from git and the transcript
Costs no usage, but the note is a file list and the last two messages, so the next session has to work out the next step itself.
Only a note I write says what to do next.
pickup
How should your other account find the work?
A
Loaded at session start from the pushed branch
You open a session on that branch, and the note loads by itself. Nothing goes outside the repo.
B
Also post it as a pull request comment
Readable from your phone without opening a session, but adds a GitHub post every time the note changes.
The note lives with the code it describes.

wrapup.summary: Every reply that changes files ends committed, pushed and described in a short handoff note, so a usage limit never strands work, on any surface. Your other account loads the note when it opens the branch.
wrapup.changing: scripts/hook.py (the save check in the Stop hook and the pickup at session start), rules/house-rules.md (one sentence), a docs/4-systems/ page, verify.py and the plugin version.
wrapup.blocking: Your approval and your three picks. Once you approve, I also create one parent issue that replaces #140 ("auto create a handoff document at 95% usage and commit all current changes"), plus one issue per step, before any code changes.
wrapup.next: Before handing it over for QA, I'll run the save check for real in a cloud session and, once your desktop app is connected to this thread, in a desktop session. Not tested and not relied on: StopFailure at a real usage limit, and whether the desktop app runs a status line.
